title: Post-Diwali Delhi Air Will Be Very Bad, Justice Vikram Nath Tells Court
excerpt: Fixing a hearing date, the Supreme Court judge said judges must attend in person while advocates can appear virtually, as GRAP Stage I is already in force and Diwali falls on November 8.
body:
• Justice Vikram Nath said in the Supreme Court on Wednesday that post-Diwali air in Delhi will be very bad and that judges cannot sit at home to escape pollution, unlike advocates who can appear virtually.
  • This year's Diwali falls on November 8; Delhi's 24-hour average AQI was 197 at 4 pm on October 27 and 228 at 7 am on October 28.
  • CAQM invoked Stage I of GRAP across Delhi-NCR on October 21 after the daily average AQI reached 244 at 2 pm and 245 at 4 pm, in the poor category.
  • Reader action under Stage I: keep PUC certificates current, do not idle vehicles, avoid firecrackers, prefer public transport or pooling, and report pollution on the 311, Green Delhi or SAMEER apps.

Delhi's air will get significantly worse after Diwali and judges cannot stay home to avoid it, Justice Vikram Nath remarked in the Supreme Court on Wednesday, in an exchange that put the capital's annual pollution season back in the courtroom before the festival has even arrived. The observation came while the court was fixing a hearing date. Senior Advocate Indira Jaising asked for a listing after the Diwali vacation, on November 17, while opposing counsel sought a date in the first week of November, according to Live Law.

Jaising said, in a lighter note, that Diwali is an extremely polluted time in Delhi. Justice Nath replied that the environment would be cleaner before Diwali and worse after it. When Jaising said she was willing to endure the pollution and appear in person, noting judges would have to come to court in any case, Justice Nath answered that advocates have the privilege of sitting at home and appearing virtually, while judges must attend physically to hold court.

"We can't sit at home. You have the privilege of sitting at home and saving yourselves from the pollution, but we can't."

— Justice Vikram Nath, Supreme Court of India

What the numbers show

Last year, Delhi's 24-hour average Air Quality Index rose from 268 on October 18, 2025, and 296 on October 19 to 345 on Diwali, October 20. It climbed further to 351 on October 21 and 353 on October 22, staying in the very poor category. This year Diwali falls on November 8. Delhi's 24-hour average AQI stood at 197 at 4 pm on October 27, 2026, with a reading of 228 recorded at 7 am on October 28.

Restrictions are already in force. The Commission for Air Quality Management invoked Stage I of the Graded Response Action Plan across Delhi-NCR on October 21, 2026, after Delhi's daily average AQI reached 244 at 2 pm and 245 at 4 pm, both in the poor category of 201 to 300, as summarised in WeNotice from the official release. Stage I sets 25 action points for agencies, covering dust control at construction sites, mechanised road sweeping and water sprinkling, a ban on open burning of waste, stricter vehicle pollution checks, and enforcement of court and tribunal orders on firecrackers.

The firecracker argument behind the remark

The Supreme Court has monitored Delhi-NCR pollution for years in the MC Mehta case, covering vehicles, industry, power plants, dust, stubble burning, waste and firecrackers. A bench in 2024 and 2025 criticised poor enforcement and directed Delhi to consider a year-round ban; Delhi imposed a comprehensive ban on December 19, 2024. In October 2025 a successor bench relaxed it for a limited Diwali window for approved green crackers.

This year, on September 30, a bench of Justice MM Sundresh and Justice Augustine George Masih said in Arjun Gopal v. Union of India that it would neither impose a complete ban nor permit unrestricted use, stressing a balance between religious sentiment and the health impact on children, older people and those with illnesses. On October 12, Chief Justice Surya Kant's bench heard the suo motu pollution proceedings, where amicus curiae Aparajita Singh argued that time limits fail if directions keep being violated.

What residents should do now

Under the Stage I Citizens Charter, residents are asked to keep engines tuned and PUC certificates up to date, switch off at red lights, avoid end-of-life and visibly polluting vehicles, prefer public transport, pooling or electric vehicles, dispose of waste only at designated points, avoid diesel generator sets except for essential use, and celebrate festivals without firecrackers. Pollution can be reported on the 311 App, Green Delhi App or SAMEER App, which also carries AQI readings. For families in Delhi and for relatives visiting for Diwali on November 8, the practical window is the fortnight after the festival, when last year's data show AQI stayed above 350: limit strenuous outdoor activity on very poor days, especially for children, older adults and anyone with respiratory illness, and check the daily AQI before planning travel or outdoor events.
